# How to read an adversarial program

The programs in this book are *adversarial* on purpose. They do things that code should not do: run code inside a regex match, call methods while parsing a markup file, rewrite their own jump targets. They are safe to study because of how this repository handles them. Every entry writes fictional **DEMO ONLY** data, runs in a [sandbox](../../SANDBOX-SETUP.md), and is reviewed as untrusted code until someone has read and understood it.

This chapter is the reader's safety model. It has two habits. First, **read the weird program next to its ordinary sibling**: [`cobol`](../../src/cobol/README.md) beside [`cobol-weird`](../../src/cobol-weird/README.md), [`haskell`](../../src/haskell/README.md) beside [`haskell-weird`](../../src/haskell-weird/README.md). The difference shows you exactly what the stunt costs. Second, **ask what kind of promise stands behind each trick**: guaranteed, implementation-permitted or accidentally exploited (see the [intro](../intro.md#three-kinds-of-knowledge)). The topics below are the security and review ideas that make those habits work. They include one that the tar entries bring out: authority comes from the command that runs a program, not from the data it reads ([Capability and authority](01-reading-an-adversarial-program.md#capability-and-authority)).

## Threat model

A threat model answers four plain questions. What are we protecting? Who might attack it? How could they do it? What will we do about that? It exists because nobody can defend against "everything". You defend against a list, and the list is the threat model. Teams use it to decide where to spend review time and which protections to add. This repository turns the usual question around. The code is the thing we do *not* trust (a pull request from a stranger), and the thing we protect is the reviewer's machine. That is why [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](../../CONTRIBUTING.md) asks for a check script that runs on a throwaway system with no network.

- **Use it when:** you are about to run, install or review code you did not write, or when you design anything that accepts input.
- **Avoid it when:** you treat it as a document you write once. A threat model that nobody updates describes a system that no longer exists.

**Two examples from this repo, where the threat model had to change:**

- **"It's just markup."** The XAML entry ([`xaml`](../../src/xaml/README.md)) directly inspired a second project, [xaml-write-and-run](https://github.com/dullroar/xaml-write-and-run). That project builds the shape of a command-and-control channel from nothing but `.xaml` files: one file writes the next file to disk, a later object in the same document loads and runs it, and the chain extends itself. A variant fetches its next instructions from the web. It rests on a well-known attack path (the classic `ObjectDataProvider` deserialization gadget), one that defenders already know and guard against. That is the lesson. Even on a well-guarded path, "it is only markup" is a false comfort: a trusted parser that reads attacker-influenced markup is running a program, so your threat model must treat markup as code.
- **"It's just a regex."** The Perl entry ([`regex-perl`](../../src/regex-perl/README.md)) is a single pattern match. Inside that match, Perl code blocks seed the data, write to a database and print, and then the match returns false on purpose. If your threat model only worries about a regex running slowly (see [Regular-expression denial of service](08-abstraction-leaks-and-implementation-dependence.md#regular-expression-denial-of-service)), update it. A regex can also run code, and a pattern deserves the same care as any other program you accept.

**Read more:**

- [Threat model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threat_model) (Wikipedia)
- [RFC 3552, section 3: the Internet threat model](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3552), a short, practical example from the IETF
- [Threat modeling](https://owasp.org/www-community/Threat_Modeling) (OWASP), a step-by-step guide

## Arbitrary code execution

Arbitrary code execution means that an attacker makes a program run instructions its author never intended. It is usually an accident: a buffer overflow, an injected string, a file format that is more powerful than anyone noticed. It matters here because many entries in this repository do the same thing *on purpose, in a safe place*. XAML's `ObjectDataProvider` calls methods while the file is parsed. Perl's `(?{ ... })` runs code in the middle of a match. Tcl's `unknown` hook runs code that is stored in a database row. The mechanism is always the same: **data is read as code**.

- **Use this idea when:** you review any feature that "evaluates" something: `eval`, templates, deserializers, macro expanders, plugin loaders.
- **Avoid the technique when:** the input comes from someone you do not trust. If you need extension points, offer a small, declared interface (a plugin API, or a tiny expression language) instead of a general `eval`.

**Read more:**

- [Arbitrary code execution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbitrary_code_execution) (Wikipedia)
- [Code injection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_injection) (Wikipedia)
- [Code injection](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/Code_Injection) (OWASP), with examples and defenses
- [`eval()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/eval) (MDN), whose page opens its warning with "Never use direct eval()!"

## Sandbox

A sandbox is a restricted place where untrusted code can run without being trusted. The code gets a small, fenced area: little memory, no network, no access to your files. It exists because "read every line first" does not scale, and because a clever program can hide what it does. Every entry here runs in one. The Linux sandbox has no network, a read-only system and an unprivileged user. Windows entries use Windows Sandbox. See [`SANDBOX-SETUP.md`](../../SANDBOX-SETUP.md).

- **Use it when:** you run code you did not write, or code that handles input you did not write.
- **Avoid trusting it blindly:** sandboxes have escape bugs, and they cannot protect the data you hand in or take out. Use one layer among several (*defense in depth*), and still read the code.

**Read more:**

- [Sandbox (computer security)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandbox_(computer_security)) (Wikipedia)
- [Operating-system-level virtualization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operating-system-level_virtualization), the idea behind containers (Wikipedia)

**In this repo:**

**Applies to every entry** (40). Every entry ships a Dockerfile for the locked-down Linux container, or a Windows Sandbox command, and its check script runs inside one of them.

## Principle of least privilege

The principle of least privilege says that every part of a system should get only the permissions it needs, and no more. It exists because every program has bugs. When a bug is exploited, the damage is limited to what that part was allowed to do. In this repository the runtime containers run as the unprivileged user `nobody`, with no network and a read-only file system. If an entry misbehaves, it has almost nothing to misbehave *with*.

- **Use it when:** always. It is the default for accounts, services, containers, API tokens and file permissions.
- **Avoid its failure mode:** if a task fails for lack of permission, grant exactly that permission. Do not "fix" it by running as root.

**Read more:**

- [Principle of least privilege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principle_of_least_privilege) (Wikipedia)
- [RFC 4949: Internet Security Glossary](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4949), which defines the term (search the page for "least privilege")

## Code review

Code review means that another person reads your code before it is accepted. It exists because tests only check what you thought to test, while a reader may notice what you did not think of. Here the review has a specific shape: the README must contain a plain-English **How the stunt works** section, and reviewers (people and AI helpers) are asked to translate the code into plain words and list everything it can touch. If the reviewer cannot follow the entry, it is not merged, however clever it is.

- **Use it when:** for every change, and most of all for unusual code.
- **Avoid relying on it alone:** tired people miss things, and invisible characters hide from eyes. Combine review with automatic checks such as `sandbox/scope-check.sh`.

**Read more:**

- [Code review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_review) (Wikipedia)

**In this repo:**

**Applies to every entry** (40). Every entry README has a How the stunt works section, the plain-English account that a reviewer reads the code against, and the gate refuses a new entry without it.

## Trojan Source: characters you cannot see

Trojan Source is an attack on the human reviewer. Unicode includes characters that you cannot see: zero-width spaces, and "bidirectional" controls that change the visual order of text. Code can *look* harmless to a person and *mean* something else to the compiler. Researchers at Cambridge described the attack in 2021 (CVE-2021-42574). This repository defends against it in a simple way: `sandbox/scope-check.sh` rejects hidden and direction-changing characters in a pull request. Visible Unicode is fine. APL needs `⍴` and `⍳`.

- **Use the defense when:** you accept code from other people. Scan for invisible characters automatically.
- **Avoid over-correcting:** do not ban all non-ASCII text. Ban the characters that have no visible shape.

**Read more:**

- [Trojan Source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trojan_Source) (Wikipedia)
- [Bidirectional text](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bidirectional_text) (Wikipedia)
- [RFC 3629: UTF-8](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3629), the encoding that carries all of this text

## Specification versus implementation

A language specification says what programs *mean*. An implementation is one particular program that tries to follow it. The two can differ, and the difference is where this book lives. Each lesson tags a trick as **guaranteed** (the specification promises it), **implementation-permitted** (one compiler or platform allows it) or **accidentally exploited** (it works today, and nobody promised it). The IETF gave engineers a useful vocabulary for the same idea: MUST, SHOULD and MAY, defined in RFC 2119. A specification that uses those words carefully tells you exactly how much you can lean on it.

- **Use it when:** before you rely on any behavior, ask which of the three kinds of promise stands behind it.
- **Avoid:** treating "it worked on my machine" as evidence, or reading a specification as a promise about speed.

**Read more:**

- [Programming language specification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_language_specification) (Wikipedia)
- [RFC 2119: key words for use in RFCs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119), two pages that fix the meaning of MUST, SHOULD and MAY
- [Undefined, unspecified and implementation-defined behavior](08-abstraction-leaks-and-implementation-dependence.md#undefined-unspecified-and-implementation-defined-behavior) and [Hyrum's law](08-abstraction-leaks-and-implementation-dependence.md#hyrums-law) in "Abstraction leaks and implementation dependence"

## Capability and authority

Who can do what is a question about **authority**, not only about data. A file that cannot do anything on its own gains power when something with authority agrees to act on it. The old rule of **capability security** is that you should hold only the authority you need, and that authority should come from what you were handed, not from what you can name.

[`tar-gnu`](../../src/tar-gnu/README.md) shows it in one line. An archive cannot register a hook for itself. `tar -xf` writes files and runs nothing, and `tar --to-command=...` starts a program for each member. The authority to run something is in the command that the *operator* typed, so the trust boundary is that command. [`ed-weird`](../../src/ed-weird/README.md) and [`ex-weird`](../../src/ex-weird/README.md) make a similar choice about the editors. GNU ed allows a shell escape (`!`) inside a global command list, and Ex has `!` and file commands too. Both programs avoid them, and their check scripts enforce that. The reason is not that the commands are bad. A program that can run a shell can do anything, and one that cannot is much easier to reason about. See also [Sandbox](01-reading-an-adversarial-program.md#sandbox) and [Principle of least privilege](01-reading-an-adversarial-program.md#principle-of-least-privilege).

- **Use it when:** you design an interface that runs something on someone's behalf. Ask what authority each caller carries, and give the callee no more.
- **Avoid it when:** you treat "it is only data" as a reason to stop thinking. Data is inert only until a consumer with authority acts on it.

**Read more:**

- [Capability-based security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capability-based_security) (Wikipedia)
- [Principle of least privilege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principle_of_least_privilege) (Wikipedia)
- [Confused deputy problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confused_deputy_problem) (Wikipedia)
